summary: States use cases and requirements for SIP-based media recording. Call centers and financial trading floors often must record calls for regulatory reasons or quality control, typically by sending a copy of the media to a recording device. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6341 describes situations where organizations record calls and lists what a SIP-based recording mechanism must support. It covers sending media and session details to a recording server while accounting for user notification, privacy, and security.

questions: what is a session recording server

subtitle: Use cases and requirements for copying SIP session media and metadata to a recording server.

tldr.problem: Organizations may need to record all or some communication sessions, but recording needs vary and can include notification, privacy, media, and availability requirements.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes twelve use cases and lists thirty-one requirements for a SIP-based Recording Session between a Session Recording Client and a Session Recording Server.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational requirements document, not the recording protocol itself. Active recording is in scope; passive recording and lawful intercept are outside scope.

today: RFC 6341 is an Informational RFC published in August 2011. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the document specifies use cases and requirements, not the SIP recording protocol.

sections.title: Why Calls Are Recorded
sections.content:
Businesses may record communication sessions for compliance, dispute resolution, quality control, or business analysis. Financial trading environments may need to record all calls, while call centers may record a selected subset. In the latter case, a call must not fail just because the recording device is unavailable.

The RFC says participants may have a right to know that a call is recorded or may be recorded, and may be able to ask that recording stop or end the call. Scenarios where participants are not informed are out of scope, as is lawful intercept. The requirements aim to allow flexibility because recording needs and costs differ among environments.
sections.plainLanguage: Some organizations record every call, while others record selected calls or parts of calls. The recording system must support the relevant business needs and let participants know when recording may take place.

sections.title: The Client, Server, and Two Sessions
sections.content:
The Session Recording Client (SRC) is the function that sends recorded media to the Session Recording Server (SRS). It may be implemented in a phone, media gateway, session border controller, or other SIP element. The SRS receives the media and session metadata.

The call among participants is the Communication Session (CS). The separate SIP session between the SRC and SRS is the Recording Session (RS). The archive may include media and metadata that describes the call, participants, and streams so the recording can be searched and played back meaningfully. The RFC covers active recording, where the SRC deliberately streams media to an SRS; it does not cover passive network capture.
sections.plainLanguage: The Communication Session is the call people have with one another. The Recording Session is a separate connection that sends a copy of its media and related information to the recorder.

sections.title: Twelve Recording Use Cases
sections.content:
The use cases cover different relationships between a call and its recording. They include recording every call, selecting calls or call segments, starting or stopping a recording during a call, and keeping one Recording Session open across multiple calls. The RFC also considers pause and resume controls, Interactive Voice Response recordings, mobile workers, centralized recording, and associated calls such as a customer call and a supervisor consultation.

Other cases require high availability, multiple media streams, synchronized recordings, or real-time media processing. A recording may combine several calls or keep participants' streams separate. These cases explain why a single fixed recording model would not serve every deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: A recording system may record every call, selected calls, or only part of a call. It may also need to handle mobile workers, multiple media streams, and real-time recording controls.

sections.title: Requirements for a Recording Mechanism
sections.content:
The RFC lists requirements REQ-001 through REQ-031. They require SIP to establish, maintain, and terminate Recording Sessions; support recording all calls, selected calls, or selected parts; and support voice, DTMF, video, and text media. Recording must not clip the beginning of a call or delay or degrade the Communication Session.

The mechanism must support pause, resume, and stop; provide call and participant metadata; correlate media with the participants; allow incremental metadata updates; and support synchronization of media, metadata, and control events. Recording-aware user agents can request recording actions subject to policy, receive notification of the outcome, and show whether recording is taking place. The requirements also cover authentication, integrity, and confidentiality for the recording connection.
sections.plainLanguage: The requirements cover what to record, how to control recording, what details to send, and how to protect the copy. They also say recording must not delay or reduce the quality of the call.

sections.title: Privacy and Security Considerations
sections.content:
Notification and opt-out rules vary by jurisdiction and deployment policy. Not every participant is necessarily authorized to stop a recording, although any participant can end their part in the call. Policies for access, use, and retention of recordings are usually set by the organization doing the recording; this RFC does not let participants dictate those policies.

The SRC and SRS need to authenticate each other, and the Recording Session's signaling and media need protection from eavesdropping. A malicious or faulty SRC could alter media or metadata before sending them; ensuring the correctness of what the SRC emits is outside the document's scope and requires other controls.
sections.plainLanguage: Participants need clear notice, and organizations need policies for access to and retention of recordings. The recording client and server must authenticate one another and protect the copied media and metadata.
